questions.stem: On a head-up radar display, what is at the top of the screen and what kind of bearing do you read off the scale?
options: The ship's heading at the top, and relative bearings
North at the top, and the bearings are true
The next waypoint at the top, and the bearings are magnetic
The wind direction at the top, and bearings are apparent
questions.explanation: Head-up puts the ship's head at the top, so bearings from the scale are relative to the bow. The picture swings when the ship yaws because it is not stabilised.

questions.stem: A radar is set to north-up. What does it need to be stabilised?
options: A speed log input only
An AIS transponder signal
A second radar on the other band
A heading input from a gyro or electronic compass
questions.explanation: North-up and other stabilised modes need to know which way the ship is pointing, so they rely on a heading signal. A wrong or frozen heading input then turns every bearing by the same error without looking wrong.

questions.stem: In course-up mode, what is held at the top of the screen?
options: Always true north
Always the ship's current heading
A chosen course, such as the intended track
The strongest echo on the screen
questions.explanation: Course-up holds the top of the screen on a selected course or direction and re-sets when a new one is chosen. It also depends on a heading input.

questions.stem: On a relative motion display with own ship fixed at the centre, how does a stationary buoy abeam appear to move as you pass it?
options: It stays still in the same place on the screen
It moves down the screen parallel to your course
It moves steadily towards the centre of the screen
It circles the centre once per antenna rotation
questions.explanation: On relative motion, everything moves relative to you. A fixed object moves in the opposite direction to your own movement, parallel to your course. On a true motion display the buoy would stay put.

questions.stem: Which is generally more accurate on a marine radar, a range or a bearing?
options: A range, as it is timed, while bearings suffer beam width
A bearing, because the antenna points exactly at the target
They are equally accurate on any modern set
Neither, because both depend on the gain setting
questions.explanation: Ranges come from timing and are good. Bearings suffer from beam width, and a typical figure is within a few degrees. That is why radar fixes use ranges first.

questions.stem: A radar has a horizontal beam width of 2 degrees. About how much wider sideways does the beam make a target echo appear at 3.0 nm?
options: About 0.01 nm
About 0.50 nm
About 3.0 nm
About 0.10 nm
questions.explanation: The spread is about range × tan(beam width) = 3.0 × tan 2° = 3.0 × 0.0349 = 0.105 nm, roughly 190 m. That is why targets look bigger than they are and nearby targets blur together.

questions.stem: Echoes appear on the bearing of a mast on your own ship, at the same range as a large target ahead, and they move in a way no real vessel would. What are they most likely?
options: Second-trace echoes from beyond the selected range scale
Genuine small craft hidden by clutter
Indirect (ghost) echoes off the ship's own structure
Side-lobe echoes caused by too little gain
questions.explanation: An indirect echo appears on the bearing of the reflecting surface, at the same range as the real target, often in a shadow sector. Second-trace echoes come from beyond the selected range scale, and side-lobe echoes form arcs either side of a large target.

questions.stem: A ship is passing on a parallel course at 1.5 nm. Fainter echoes appear on the same bearing at 3.0 nm and 4.5 nm. What are they?
options: Real ships following one another in line astern
Multiple echoes at multiples of the true range
Side-lobe echoes from the passing ship
Racon replies from a nearby mark
questions.explanation: Multiple echoes appear on the bearing of the real target at two, three or more times its range, each weaker than the last, typically when another vessel passes close on a parallel course.

questions.stem: Which is a typical sign of side-lobe echoes?
options: An arc of echoes either side of a large, close target
A single extra echo at half the true range
A row of echoes at exact multiples of range on one bearing
A radial line starting just beyond a buoy
questions.explanation: Side-lobe echoes form arcs at the same range as a large target, mostly at short range. A row at multiples of range is a multiple echo, and a radial line beyond a mark is a racon.

questions.stem: A funnel and a crane block part of the radar beam. What risk does this create?
options: Every echo is displayed at twice its range
Gain is automatically doubled in that sector
The heading marker stops working while it is blocked
A small near target in that sector may be missed
questions.explanation: A shadow or blind sector reduces beam intensity behind the obstruction. Small close targets there can be missed, so know your ship's blind arcs and cover them with the look-out.

questions.stem: Which target is likely to give the strongest radar echo?
options: A fibreglass boat seen end-on
A wooden boat seen end-on
A steel vessel seen broadside
A smooth, low sand beach
questions.explanation: Metal reflects better than wood or fibreglass, and a vessel broadside to the radar returns more than one end-on. Low smooth beaches may not show beyond a mile or two.

questions.stem: A pulse of 0.5 microsecond is used, at about 164 yards of distortion per microsecond of pulse length. By about how much is a target stretched in range?
options: About 8 yards
About 82 yards
About 328 yards
About 1 nautical mile
questions.explanation: Half the pulse length is the minimum radial stretch: 0.5 × 164 = 82 yards, about 75 m. Doubling it to 328 yards would treat the pulse as a full round trip, and the other values are far off.
